scenes.heading: GORM: Models, Queries & Associations
scenes.narration: GORM is Go's most popular ORM. Let's see how it maps structs to tables, and learn the sharp edges before they bite you.

scenes.heading: What GORM gives you
items: Structs are your schema; embed gorm.Model for ID and timestamps
Open once at startup, AutoMigrate, share the *gorm.DB
It's a thin layer over database/sql — the pool still needs tuning
scenes.narration: You describe your schema as ordinary structs, and embedding gorm.Model adds an ID, created and updated timestamps, and a soft-delete field. You open one gorm.DB at startup, call AutoMigrate to reconcile tables with your structs, and share that handle across every goroutine. Crucially, GORM is a thin layer over database/sql, so the underlying connection pool still needs the same tuning you'd give raw SQL.

scenes.heading: The everyday verbs
steps: Create inserts and back-fills the primary key
Delete soft-deletes when DeletedAt is present
scenes.narration: The daily vocabulary is small. Create inserts a row and back-fills its primary key. First fetches one record and Find scans many. Where builds the predicate. Updates writes changed columns. And Delete, when your model has the DeletedAt field, is a soft delete: it sets deleted-at and future queries automatically hide the row.

scenes.heading: Defeating the N+1 problem
scenes.narration: Here is the single most impactful GORM skill. GORM does not lazy-load struct fields, so if you Find a slice of users and then loop to load each user's posts, you fire one query per user — the N-plus-one problem that destroys latency as data grows. Preload fixes it by eager-loading every association in one batched query using WHERE user-id IN. For a belongs-to relation, Joins folds it into a single query instead.

scenes.text: Updates with a struct SKIPS zero-values — false, 0, and "" are never written.
scenes.narration: And beware the famous gotcha: Updates given a struct silently skips zero-value fields. Setting Active to false does nothing, because false is the zero value for a bool, so the update reports success while the change is dropped. The fix is to pass a map, or to Select the column explicitly.

scenes.text: Master models, Preload/Joins, and transactions — and drop to db.Raw when the builder can't express it.
scenes.narration: So master the model, query, and association trio, reach for Preload or Joins on list endpoints, wrap multi-statement writes in a transaction, and drop to raw SQL when the fluent builder is awkward. Do that and you get fast development without losing control of the database.
